en: Jātaka: The Eighth Book of Birth Stories (Aṭṭhakanipāta),
Chapter on Kaccāyana (Kaccānivagga)
8. The Āditta Jātaka:
“In a house that is on fire, whatever vessel one carries out;”
That is for his benefit,
and not that which is burned therein;
even so is the world set ablaze.
By means of giving, one should indeed carry it away from old age and death;
what is given is truly well-carried away.
“The person who gives a gift obtained by righteous means,
acquired through exertion and effort;
having crossed over Yama’s Vetaraṇī river, they shall not grieve.”
A mortal attains divine realms.
They say that giving and battle are alike:
even those who are few conquer many.
If one gives even a little with faith,
by that alone one becomes happy in the next world.
Giving after careful discernment is praised by the Sugata.
Those who are worthy of offerings in this world of the living—
to them, gifts given yield great fruit,
just as seeds sown in a fertile field.
One who wanders without harming living beings and does no evil through slandering others—
such a person is praised as "timid," not as a "hero" in that regard.
For out of fear, the virtuous do not commit evil.
Through an inferior holy life,
one is reborn among the Khattiyas.
Through moderate [giving] one attains the state of the gods,
and through supreme [giving] one is purified.
Indeed, giving is praised in many ways.
But the verse of the Dhamma is indeed better than giving;
for those who were wise have, from of old and even earlier,
attained nothing other than Nibbāna.
The Ādittajātaka, the eighth.
